after: ## Indicators: what each one tells you
alt: Life expectancy, education and income feed into the Human Development Index, a composite value from 0 to 1. Below, two cases show why one indicator misleads: an oil-rich country with high GNP per capita but low literacy among women, and a modest-income country with high life expectancy from good primary health care.
caption: A composite index reduces the distortion of any one measure.

after: ## Worked example 1: comparing countries with data
alt: Bar charts for three illustrative countries. GNP per capita: P 45,000, Q 12,000, R 1,500 US dollars, so P is 30 times R. Life expectancy: 82, 76 and 62 years, a 20-year gap between P and R. Adult literacy: 99, 94 and 55 per cent. Q has about a quarter of P’s income but only 6 years’ lower life expectancy.
caption: Turn figures into comparisons: “30 times”, “20 years longer”.

alt: A schematic country with a core region around the capital and a port on the coast, and a periphery of scattered rural houses. Young workers migrate from the periphery to the core. Beside it a cycle: markets and ports already exist, investment and infrastructure go there, jobs draw young workers in, and the core grows while the periphery lags. Examples: south-east versus north-east Brazil, coastal versus interior China, and urban–rural gaps.
caption: Investment follows existing markets, workers follow investment, and the gap widens.

alt: Three stages. Low development: most people work in the primary sector, largely subsistence farming, with little capital or technology. Industrialising: farm machinery releases labour, factory jobs pay more and TNC investment builds factories, so the secondary sector grows. High development: rising incomes create demand for services and manufacturing is automated or moved abroad, so tertiary and quaternary jobs dominate.
caption: Each shift has a cause: give it, then its effect on jobs.

alt: Four drivers (transport, information and communication technology, TNCs, and trade agreements) feed into globalisation, the growing connection and interdependence of economies through trade, investment, migration and information. Positives: jobs and investment, skills and technology, cheaper goods, export earnings. Negatives: low wages in some factories, profits leaving, local firms out-competed, job losses on relocation, environmental damage.
caption: A globalisation answer needs both columns and a judgement.

after: ## Worked example 2: building a TNC case study
alt: Toyota’s headquarters and research in Toyota City, Japan, link to three overseas plants: a car plant at Burnaston near Derby and an engine plant at Deeside in North Wales (UK), and a large plant at Georgetown, Kentucky (USA). Reasons for locating abroad: inside major markets, avoiding tariffs, lower transport costs, skilled workers. Host impacts: jobs, a multiplier effect, training and exports, but decisions and profits stay in Japan.
caption: Learn a headquarters, named overseas sites, reasons, and one impact each way.
